planting.note: Scarify and inoculate seed with the specific kura-clover rhizobium strain before drilling shallowly into a firm, weed-free seedbed; stands spread by rhizomes but typically need a full year or more before closing in, so pair with a nurse crop or mow competing weeds during establishment.

directions: Rhizo was released in 1989 by the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Materials Center at Quicksand, Kentucky, selected for vigorous, strongly rhizomatous spread aimed at long-term pasture and cover applications in the Appalachian region. Unlike white clover, it establishes slowly from hard, dormant seed and may take more than a season to form a closed sod, but once set it persists for many years under grazing or mowing with little reseeding needed. Its deep, rhizome-fed root system builds soil structure and fixes nitrogen steadily over time, making it better suited to permanent cover in orchards, pastures, or living mulches than to a fast single-season rotation. Mow or graze lightly in the establishment year to limit weed competition while the rhizome network develops.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Materials Program
University of Minnesota Extension — Kura Clover for Pasture and Cover
USDA Agricultural Research Service Forage Legume Research

planting.note: Scarify and inoculate hard-coated seed and drill no deeper than half an inch into a clean seedbed in early spring; like alfalfa it is slow out of the ground and should not be grazed or cut hard in the seeding year.

directions: Windsor was released through USDA-ARS forage-legume breeding work and registered in 1994 as an improved cicer milkvetch. It spreads slowly by creeping rhizomes into a dense, non-bloating perennial stand, so it is more often used as a long-term rangeland and cover legume than a quick-turnaround rotational crop. Because its foliage does not cause the bloat risk that alfalfa can in grazing livestock, it is a useful nitrogen-fixing companion in mixed pasture or conservation plantings on the northern Plains. Expect a thin first-year stand with full ground cover and nitrogen contribution building over the following one to two seasons.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service Forage and Range Research Laboratory
Crop Science journal — cultivar registration notices
Montana State University Extension — Cicer Milkvetch for Pasture and Conservation

planting.note: Inoculate and scarify seed before a shallow spring planting on well-drained, coarser-textured ground; Oxley is slower to close its canopy than clover and benefits from a clean, low-competition seedbed.

directions: Oxley is an older western Canadian cicer milkvetch cultivar, a creeping-rooted, non-bloating perennial legume later used as the comparison standard for the improved release 'AC Oxley II'. It performs best on coarse-textured to alkaline range and pasture soils where few other legumes persist, tolerating cold winters and extended drought once its rhizome network is established. As a cover and forage legume, it fixes nitrogen gradually over several seasons rather than in one quick cycle, so it fits long-term conservation plantings and mixed grass-legume pastures better than annual rotations. Allow a full establishment year with light or no grazing before relying on it for forage or ground cover.
sources: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada — Forage Legume Breeding Program
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Fact Sheet — Cicer Milkvetch

subcategory: cool-season annual to short-lived perennial grass

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into a prepared seedbed in early fall so seedlings reach a grazable or mowable stage before the coldest weather; it grows most actively through the mild Gulf South winter and into spring.

directions: Matua is a New Zealand-bred selection of prairie grass, a cool-season bunchgrass native to the South American pampas that behaves as a reseeding winter annual to short-lived perennial depending on climate. In the Gulf South it fills the late-fall-through-spring window with fast, leafy growth that outpaces many small grains, giving quick soil cover and a palatable grazing or hay option ahead of summer crops. It tolerates wetter, heavier soils better than annual ryegrass and will reseed itself where seedheads are allowed to mature before the first hard summer heat sets in. Mow or graze periodically to keep it vegetative, since unchecked growth lodges and loses forage quality quickly.
sources: Kansas State University Research and Extension — Matua Prairie Grass
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Cool-Season Grasses for Winter Forage
Oregon State University Seed Certification Service variety notes

planting.note: Plant hulled, debearded seed shallowly into warm soil after the last frost; establishment is slow the first year, so control weed competition and avoid grazing or mowing hard until the bunchgrass crowns are well rooted.

directions: Selection 75 was released in 1969 through the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station and the Soil Conservation Service as an introduced African bunchgrass adapted to heavy clay rangeland across central and south Texas. It is notably drought tolerant once established and tolerates heat and periodic flooding better than many native warm-season grasses, though it winterkills more readily on sandy, excessively drained sites. As a cover crop it provides deep-rooted perennial ground cover and erosion control on tight soils where few other grasses perform well, rather than functioning as a quick rotational green manure. Give it a full growing season to establish before grazing or haying it hard.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service James E. 'Bud' Smith Plant Materials Center
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Kleingrass for Range and Pasture
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Panicum coloratum

planting.note: Plant shallowly into warm, firm soil once frost danger has passed; this cultivar carries slightly larger seed than older kleingrass selections, which helps even seed drop and stand uniformity from a drill.

directions: Verde was released around 1981-82 from the same Texas Agricultural Experiment Station and James E. 'Bud' Smith Plant Materials Center program that produced Selection 75, selected for broader leaves, a somewhat larger plant, and bigger seed size while keeping comparable forage quality and seed production. It shares Selection 75's preference for tight clay soils and drought tolerance across Texas rangeland, making it a substitute or companion where a leafier, easier-to-establish stand is wanted. As a perennial warm-season cover it anchors heavy ground against erosion through summer heat once rooted in, though it is not suited to deep, loose sand where winterkill risk is higher. Allow a full season of establishment before cutting or grazing it closely.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service James E. 'Bud' Smith Plant Materials Center
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Kleingrass for Range and Pasture
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Panicum coloratum
